clue.text: I'm not one to think he will pass gas, Bill

indicators.note: he will pass gas, so he comes after it in the answer

parts.note: air is a gas, the stuff we breathe
AD is short for advertisement, a bill or poster

explanation.surface: A man about to break wind, then a person called Bill, in an apparently crude remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will pass' is a placing signal: he comes along after the gas. The surface tempts a reading about breaking wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A scatterbrained person proverbially does little thinking, so the clue's self-description fits such a fool.

clue.text: Is Hoskins gifted with a friendly demeanour?

parts.note: said by the setter of himself, 'is' becomes the first-person form am
Hoskins is the setter, who calls himself I
gifted means capable, able

explanation.surface: The setter wonders whether he is talented, while friendliness is mentioned in passing.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for the first person: 'Is Hoskins gifted?' becomes 'Am I able?' from his own mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone affable and pleasant has a friendly manner, which is the adjective's plain sense.

clue.text: Desire to have Congress send Iran new spades

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of these words are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A political demand that the US legislature dispatch fresh shovels to Iran.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges SENDIRAN into RANDINES. 'Congress' looks like the US parliament; here it means sexual intercourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustfulness is an urge for sexual intercourse, which is the old sense of congress used here.

clue.text: Furious English editor taking on national paper

indicators.note: the editor takes on the other pieces, joining them at the end

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: An angry English editor hires a reporter from a national newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking on' makes ED take the preceding letters with it, so it ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being furious and being incensed are synonyms for extreme anger.

clue.text: Fellow's bitter about Tory leader? Give over!

indicators.note: the fellow's letters go about the Tory leader, enclosing it

parts.note: a fellow of a college is a don; fellow's is read as dons

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, here of Tory

parts.note: tart means sour or bitter

explanation.surface: Someone resents a Conservative chief, and an exasperated listener tells them to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts T inside DONS to make DONTS. 'Give over!' is British slang for 'stop it!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are exclamations telling someone to stop going on about something, a colloquial equivalent.

clue.text: Party without tinnies? It's not possible!

parts.note: without means having no, giving no
tinnies is slang for cans of beer, giving can
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A party without beer cans is unthinkable, someone exclaims.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the order 'without tinnies' then 'Party': a no-can do.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial refusal meaning a thing simply cannot be done.

clue.text: Celtic hooligans cuddling right geeky types

indicators.note: cuddling means the hooligans' letters wrap around the other piece

parts.note: ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan

explanation.surface: Scottish football thugs hug a correct bunch of geeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celtic' suggests the Glasgow football club, but it just places the slang word NED in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerds and geeks are synonyms for socially awkward, studious enthusiasts.

clue.text: Medical examiner promoting first Queen, then Crosby?

indicators.note: promoting first moves the Queen's letter up towards the front

parts.note: a coroner examines deaths
R is for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A doctor pushes the Queen up the queue, followed by a famous singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promoting first' moves R up two places in CORONER. Bing Crosby was a famous American singer of soft ballads.
explanation.definitionFit: Bing Crosby is the classic example of a soft-voiced ballad singer, hence the question mark.

clue.text: What you'll get from one piercing hooter?

definitions.text: What you'll get from one piercing hooter?

indicators.note: piercing means the single letter goes through the nose's letters

parts.note: hooter is slang for the nose
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A shrill car horn produces a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, a piercing hooter (horn) makes a din; read as wordplay, I pierces NOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud horn produces a din, and a din is exactly an unpleasant sound.

clue.text: Done up fronts of terraces awfully, eh? Stuff yourself!

parts.note: done means finished, over

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the fronts of these words are their first letters

explanation.surface: Someone does up the house fronts on a terrace badly and tells another to get stuffed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns TAE (first letters of 'terraces awfully, eh') into EAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff yourself is to gorge, taking in more food than you need.

clue.text: The champ getting scalped is something to aim for in archery

definitions.text: something to aim for in archery

indicators.note: scalped means losing the top of the head, so the first letter goes

parts.note: the champion is the winner

explanation.surface: A champion archer suffers a grisly fate while the target is mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting scalped' drops the W from WINNER.
explanation.definitionFit: The ring just outside the bullseye on an archery target is named for its position near the centre.

clue.text: Drug reactions presented differently

indicators.note: presented differently means the letters of the word are set out in another order

explanation.surface: Side effects of a medicine show up in a new form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drug' is a verb here, not the noun the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To narcotise someone is to put them under the influence of a narcotic, which is to drug them.

clue.text: Narrow raised lines on black crosses

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another follows it, so the lines come after black

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
ridges are narrow raised strips

explanation.surface: Describes a pattern of thin embossed lines over black crosses.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'on' puts RIDGES after B.
explanation.definitionFit: To span a river is to cross it, so the verb fits a third-person 'crosses'.

clue.text: In Kent, I caught the Queen astride knight, honest

indicators.note: in Kent means the rest sits inside the letters for south-east

parts.note: Kent is a county in South-East England, SE

indicators.note: astride means the preceding letters straddle the knight's letter

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
ER is Elizabeth Regina
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A cricketer in Kent boasts of catching the Queen on horseback beside a knight, and swears it's true.
explanation.walkthrough: 'astride' splits ICER around N into INCER; 'In' puts that inside SE. Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sincere and honest are synonyms for meaning what one says.

clue.text: Aim to strangle yours truly? Correct

indicators.note: strangling means the aim's letters wrap tight around the other piece

parts.note: an end is a goal or aim
yours truly is the speaker, me

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the goal is to throttle them, and is told yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct' looks like a reply of 'yes'; it is the verb, to put right.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend a text is to correct its errors, a synonym in editing.

clue.text: Town back embarrassed City with strike on goal

indicators.note: back means the letters are run in reverse order

parts.note: embarrassed means red in the face
LA, Los Angeles, is a city
a strike on goal in football is a shot

explanation.surface: A football report: a defender is shown up as City face a shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns REDLA into ALDER. Aldershot is a garrison town in Hampshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: Aldershot is an English town in Hampshire, famous as a home of the British Army.

clue.text: Diced meat supply reduced very heavily

indicators.note: supply is read as 'in a supple way', so the letters are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A butcher's stock of chopped meat has run very low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a noun but is the adverb from supple, the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: In modern usage decimated means drastically cut down, from the Roman practice of killing one in ten.

clue.text: Bug in locks of Spooner's radiation-proof dwelling?

indicators.note: Spooner's means the first sounds of the two words are swapped

parts.note: lead blocks radiation
a house is a dwelling

explanation.surface: A tiny insect lives in someone's hair, which the reverend imagines as a lead-lined home.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the starts of LEAD HOUSE gives the answer. 'locks' means hair, not door fastenings.
explanation.definitionFit: This tiny insect parasite lives in human hair, so it is literally a bug in the locks.

clue.text: Artistic set cheat badly, taking one in

indicators.note: taking in means the scrambled letters enclose the other piece
in, completing 'taking one in', says the single letter goes inside
badly means the letters of these words are put in a poor order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A creative group cheats clumsily and swindles someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' rearranges SETCHEAT, and 'taking in' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesthetic relates to beauty and art, so it means artistic in taste.

clue.text: Wasted friar admitted to A&E: cost of getting high?

indicators.note: admitted to means the jumbled letters are taken inside the hospital's letters

parts.note: A&E is the British hospital accident and emergency department

indicators.note: wasted, as in drunk, means the letters of the word are scrambled

explanation.surface: A drunk monk ends up in casualty, and someone asks what it cost to get so high.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' and 'admitted to' are the two signals. A&E is the British hospital casualty department; 'getting high' means flying, not drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane fare is the price paid to fly, which playfully is getting high in the sky.

clue.text: A brave woman taking an opiate orally

indicators.note: orally signals that the word sounds the same when spoken

parts.note: heroin is an opiate drug

explanation.surface: A courageous woman takes a narcotic by mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orally' looks like a way of taking a drug; it signals a soundalike.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman admired for courage is the female counterpart of a hero.

clue.text: Fish or an unsmoked bit of joint

definitions.meaning: a common freshwater fish of the carp family
slang for the filter end of a cannabis cigarette, left unsmoked

explanation.surface: A choice between a fish and the butt of a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: 'joint' suggests meat, as if a fish or unsmoked ham; it is a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: One word names both a carp-family fish and, in slang, the butt of a marijuana cigarette.

clue.text: Russia's premier able to be seen topless? Ludicrous!

indicators.note: the premier of a word is its first letter
topless means losing its top, the first letter

parts.note: something able to be seen is visible

explanation.surface: The Russian prime minister able to be seen without a shirt is laughable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topless' drops V from VISIBLE. 'premier' suggests a prime minister but just picks R.
explanation.definitionFit: Laughable and ludicrous are synonyms for absurdly funny.

clue.text: Ghastly skin? Common sense to not show face?

parts.note: a hide is an animal's skin

indicators.note: not showing face means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: nous is British slang for common sense

explanation.surface: Someone with dreadful skin sensibly keeps their face hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to not show face' drops the N from NOUS; nous is everyday British for good sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Hideous and ghastly are synonyms for horribly ugly.

clue.text: Secret: I redden around the middle in bed

indicators.note: around the middle says the letters are found within the run of these words

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they blush at the waist while lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around the middle' looks like a description of blushing; it marks the letters inside 'Secret: I redden'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having retired for the night means having gone to bed, so it describes being in bed.

clue.text: Time to question the leadership of Steve Jobs?

parts.note: to ask is to question

indicators.note: the leadership of a word is its first letter, here of Steve

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it is time to challenge Steve Jobs as head of Apple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steve Jobs' reads as the Apple founder, but 'Jobs' is the definition, plain duties.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks and jobs are synonyms for pieces of work to be done.

clue.text: Fear no more, the last of beer's brought aboard

indicators.note: brought aboard means taken inside the other letters

parts.note: no more means dead, as in the famous parrot

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Sailors are told not to be afraid, the final beer has been loaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought aboard' puts R inside DEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Dread and fear are synonyms, as nouns or verbs, for being afraid.

clue.text: Thought to drink first third of claret with a six pack?

indicators.note: to drink means the thought's letters swallow the others

parts.note: mused means thought, pondered

indicators.note: the first third of the six-letter word is its opening two letters

explanation.surface: Someone thought to drink some red wine with a six-pack of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to drink' is the container signal. 'six pack' sounds like beer cans but means well-defined abdominal muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: A six-pack is a set of well-defined abdominal muscles, so someone with one is brawny.

clue.text: It's a bent to get drunk around first of November, taking part in Go Sober for October?

definitions.text: taking part in Go Sober for October?

indicators.note: around means the jumbled letters surround the other piece
getting drunk means the letters of these words reel into a new order
the first of a word is its initial letter

explanation.surface: Someone inclined to drink heavily in early November joins a sobriety campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get drunk' rearranges ITSABENT, and 'around' puts N inside. Go Sober for October is a UK charity month of not drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: People doing the October challenge refrain from alcohol, which describes being teetotal.

clue.text: Manage to visit contrary old boy, Frank?

indicators.note: visiting means going inside the other letters
contrary means the letters go the opposite way

parts.note: to run something is to manage it

explanation.surface: Someone manages to call on an awkward former pupil and speak candidly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contrary' and 'to visit' are the signals. Frank Bruno is a British former heavyweight boxing champion, so 'Frank' is a name, not candour.
explanation.definitionFit: Frank Bruno is a well-known British boxer, so his surname defines by example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: A place where residents can drop off letters?

definitions.text: A place where residents can drop off letters?

parts.words: A place where residents can drop off letters?
parts.note: a post office image hides the Cockney habit of dropping the h sound from words

explanation.surface: Describes a neighbourhood with a convenient postbox.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, the traditional residents of this part of London, are famous for dropping aitches: they drop letters from speech.
explanation.definitionFit: This working-class district of London is the home of Cockney speech, known for dropped h sounds.

clue.text: One feeding puts off those trying not to!

indicators.note: feeding means the single letter is fed into the other word

parts.note: deters means puts off, discourages
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A person eating discourages others who are attempting to abstain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'those trying not to' completes the clue: those trying not to feed.
explanation.definitionFit: People on a weight-loss regime are trying not to eat much, which the clue phrases as trying not to feed.
